title: Competing for the Future
author: Gary Hamel and C. K. Prahalad
theme: Lasting success comes not from cutting costs or defending today's market share but from imagining tomorrow's industries and building the capabilities to lead them first.
summary: Gary Hamel and C. K. Prahalad wrote this book at a time when many large companies were busy downsizing, restructuring and reengineering. Their argument is that such efforts, however necessary, only help a firm catch up. Cutting people and assets shrinks the denominator of return on investment without growing the numerator, and no company can shrink its way to greatness.

The authors urge managers to stop competing only for market share in existing industries and to start competing for opportunity share in the industries of the future. That contest is won years before products reach customers, by the firms that see where needs, technologies and lifestyles are heading.

This calls for industry foresight: a well-informed view of how the competitive landscape could change over the next decade. To develop it, senior managers must challenge the unspoken assumptions, or orthodoxies, that shaped their past success. The authors note that top teams spend very little time building a shared picture of the future.

Foresight is then turned into strategic intent, an ambitious goal that stretches the organisation well beyond its current resources and gives everyone a common sense of direction. The gap between ambition and resources is meant to drive creativity rather than despair. Firms close it through resource leverage: concentrating effort, borrowing and combining resources, reusing what they learn, and getting products to market quickly.

A strategic architecture acts as a high-level blueprint, showing which new capabilities and customer interfaces must be built to reach the future. At its heart are core competencies, bundles of skills and technologies that give access to many markets and are hard for rivals to copy. Leaders should manage the company as a portfolio of competencies, not just a set of business units.
Finally, the authors stress that shaping a new industry often means building coalitions, setting standards and pre-empting rivals with early experiments.
takeaway: Spend less energy shrinking today's business and more on building the foresight, intent and core competencies that let you create tomorrow's markets.

questions.q: What is the authors' main criticism of downsizing and reengineering?
options: They are illegal in most countries
They always raise costs
They help a firm catch up but cannot by themselves create future growth
They focus too much on new markets
questions.why: Hamel and Prahalad see restructuring as shrinking the denominator, which improves ratios without building tomorrow's revenues.

questions.q: Instead of only fighting for market share, firms should compete for:
options: Opportunity share in future markets
Lower wage costs
Government contracts
A larger head office
questions.why: The book argues that the decisive contest is for a share of the opportunities emerging in future industries.

questions.q: What do the authors mean by industry foresight?
options: Precise sales forecasts for next quarter
Copying the market leader's products
Hiring consultants to predict stock prices
A deep understanding of how trends in technology, needs and lifestyles could reshape an industry
questions.why: Foresight is an informed view of possible industry change, not a narrow numerical forecast.

questions.q: Why must senior managers challenge their industry's orthodoxies?
options: To reduce the number of meetings
Because assumptions behind past success can blind them to future opportunities
Because regulators require it
To please shareholders in the short term
questions.why: Unquestioned beliefs about how an industry works keep firms from seeing new ways to compete.

questions.q: Strategic intent is best described as:
options: A detailed annual budget
A list of cost-cutting targets
An ambitious, stretching goal that gives the whole organisation a shared direction
A legal statement of company ownership
questions.why: It sets an aspiration far beyond current resources and rallies people around a common destination.

questions.q: How do the authors suggest firms close the gap between ambition and limited resources?
options: By waiting until resources grow naturally
Through resource leverage, such as concentrating, combining and reusing resources
By lowering their goals
By acquiring every competitor
questions.why: Leverage lets a resource-poor firm achieve more by using what it has more creatively and efficiently.

questions.q: What is a strategic architecture in this book?
options: The design of the company's headquarters
The organisation chart
A detailed five-year financial plan
A broad blueprint of the capabilities and customer interfaces needed to reach the future
questions.why: It maps, at a high level, what must be built now to capture tomorrow's opportunities.

questions.q: Which feature best defines a core competence?
options: A combination of skills and technologies that opens access to many markets and is hard to imitate
A single best-selling product
A large marketing budget
A low-cost factory location
questions.why: Core competencies are integrated capabilities that support multiple businesses and resist copying.

questions.q: The authors advise leaders to view the company as:
options: A collection of independent profit centres only
A portfolio of core competencies as well as business units
A pure financial holding company
A single-product enterprise
questions.why: Seeing the firm through its competencies helps leaders build and deploy capabilities across business boundaries.

questions.q: Which of these is a way of shaping a new industry that the book highlights?
options: Avoiding all partnerships
Delaying entry until the market is mature
Building coalitions and running early market experiments
Focusing only on existing customers' stated requests
questions.why: Firms that form alliances, set standards and learn through early experiments can pre-empt rivals in emerging markets.
